angle: The combo sheet says nineteen infinites; the record says Hapatra is a mint — a turn-2 commander who cashes other cards' -1/-1 counters into Snakes, cards and table-wide drain, with exactly one verified true infinite sitting above a very strong grindy median.

teases: Mikaeus + Devoted Druid loops forever — and makes exactly zero mana
Feed a Snake to Mikaeus and nothing comes back: undying on a token is a dead grant
Turn-2 commander in 9,970 of 10,000 seeded runs
36 lands, zero enter tapped — the audit finally gets to gloat

departments.headline: RUN THE MINT
departments.dek: Why does a 2/2 that never wants to attack keep winning long games? Because Hapatra is a mint, not an engine — other cards place the counters, she pays you a deathtouch Snake per placement, and every Snake becomes a card or a drain.

callouts.title: LAND THE MINT
callouts.text: Hapatra costs two and arrives on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 seeded runs. Your opening hand never needs her — it needs lands and a route to a counter source.

callouts.title: FIND THE SOURCE
callouts.text: The scarce class is two cards deep: Yawgmoth, and Devoted Druid under Mikaeus. Eight tutors exist to fix exactly that. Fetch the source before the payoff, every time.

callouts.title: CASH THE BODIES
callouts.text: Skullclamp, Grim Haruspex and Village Rites turn Snakes into cards. Out-card three opponents first. The drain converter closes once the table's interaction is counted and spent.

pilot_tips.text: Hold Fume Spitter until it does three jobs at once — a Snake, a dead X/1, and a body for a sacrifice cost.

captions.Hapatra, Vizier of Poisons: **THE MINT:** one Snake per placement event, not per counter — Black Sun's Zenith for one across six creatures mints six Snakes; for three on one creature, just one.
captions.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: **THE SOURCE:** the only free repeatable -1/-1 source in the 99 — and his single 'target' means a second body is mandatory, or you don't even draw.

departments.pull_quote: She doesn't make the counters. She sets the exchange rate.

departments.headline: ROUTE OR RERACK
departments.dek: The keep test is one question: is there a route to a repeatable counter source? Ledger's receipts say you keep 79.9% of first sevens — so be picky. You can afford it.

hands.why: Three lands, a turn-1 dork, the one free repeatable source in the 99, and two ways to cash it. Hapatra waits in the zone — this hand holds the card the zone can't promise.

A two-lander carries with a dork attached, and Demonic Tutor is any card — the census answer is one fetch away. Keep Blowfly as what it reliably is, a counter source for the grind, never half of an unverified kill.

Four lands, three converters, nothing placing counters. The goldfish keeps this hand — its rule only counts lands — and you are smarter than the goldfish: these are blanks waiting for a card you haven't drawn yet.

hands.verdict: SHIP — one land and a prayer
hands.why: A Petal that finds no second land loses the commander, and Mikaeus is your only six-drop — a combo piece for two named partners, not a plan. Mean mulligans run 0.243; shipping this is what the average is made of.

pilot_tips.text: Count Lotus Petal as a spell you're owed, not a land you have — a mox hand with one land is still a ship.

captions.Bitterblossom: **THE FREE KEEP:** a body every upkeep for 1 life — it rebuilds through wraths on its own, so it's a keepable engine all by itself.

departments.headline: YOUR CALL FIRST
departments.dek: This is the section where you commit before we do: a real board, a hard question, and our call sealed until you've made yours. The docket for this deck is still being argued — the first case up is whether Yawgmoth hits the table into open mana.

pilot_tips.text: Never present Yawgmoth into open mana unless this turn converts — he dies on sight everywhere competent.

departments.note: decisions/ is empty; the renderer shows the standing TODO. Two spreads are queued in gaps — the copy above frames the format so the promise survives the wait.

departments.headline: HARMLESS UNTIL PROVEN GUILTY
departments.dek: What does the table see? A two-mana 2/2 and a few 1/1 Snakes — the quietest board in the pod. How long they keep believing it is entirely a sequencing decision, and it's yours.

callouts.title: THE COVER
callouts.text: Deathtouch Snakes read as defense, and they are — every attacker trades down into a token that cost you nothing. Lead with the token half and the cheap counter sources.

callouts.title: THE TELL
callouts.text: Eleven Game Changers live in this list. The moment a Mox, a Demonic Tutor or The One Ring resolves, the Snakes stop reading as chump blockers. Spend loud cards on turns that convert, and fire tutors while someone else is doing something louder.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: The flip to archenemy is never Hapatra — it's the second permanent. Yawgmoth with a spare body, or Mikaeus alongside Devoted Druid or Walking Ballista, and the table is correct to dogpile you. Go the turn you're protected, or don't go.

pilot_tips.text: Cast The One Ring when you want the cards, not when you want the protection turn to look clever — it is the loudest card you own.

captions.Orcish Bowmasters: **THE QUIET MENACE:** flash it in on an opponent's draw spell — rare instant-speed interaction that spends none of your cover.

departments.pull_quote: The table isn't wrong to fear the second permanent. Make sure it's the last thing they see coming.

departments.headline: DEATHTOUCH IS A POLICY
departments.dek: Aggro can't swing into you and midrange can't out-grind you — so which board should actually scare you? The one with no creatures and a Winter Orb. Rank threats by permanent class before you rank them by size.

threats.read: The hard truth: your interaction covers exactly one permanent class, and it isn't theirs. A resolved Sphere, Orb or hoser stays forever — you race it or you politick it. Your engines cost no mana once assembled, your commander lands turn 2, and honesty about the hole is your best trade bait: say you can't answer it, and ask the seat holding the removal to spend it.

You can only interact with creature-based kills, and against combo held answers rot — the last profitable moment is now. Don't plan to out-race a dedicated combo deck either: your own headline assembly runs 16.3% and unverified. Be the seat their interaction isn't pointed at, and know your Game Changers spend that cover fast.

Your token half is nearly free to lose — Bitterblossom rebuilds every upkeep, Skullclamp and Grim Haruspex cash the deaths, and a wrath with Blood Artist out is a drain aimed wherever you like. But the half that wins is all creatures. Deploy in waves, hold the enabler until the pivot, and know your own sweepers differ: Black Sun's Zenith is a rebuild that mints Snakes; Toxic Deluge places nothing and feeds no one.

A 1/1 deathtouch Snake blanks any attacker, and a board of them blanks three attack plans at once — the cheapest answer to roughly 120 life of aggression ever printed. Track the one clock that's actually real, defend that seat only, and spend life like the resource this deck already treats it as.

The seat this deck was built for. Their removal is bad against tokens, their attacks are bad into deathtouch, and Crumbling Ashes plus any counter source is a repeating removal engine most fair decks can't touch. Out-card them with the bodies-to-cards layer, then pivot on a counted window — not a pretty board.

pilot_tips.text: Sequence Toxic Deluge as the panic button it is — until-end-of-turn -X/-X places no counters, so it mints nothing and feeds no one.

departments.pull_quote: An answer only counts when it matches a threat that actually beats you.

departments.headline: SAME WISH, EIGHT LAMPS
departments.dek: Why do eight tutors keep fetching the same card? Because the class that wins you the game is two cards deep — and a two-deep class with eight finders plays like a deep one. Know your delivery speeds: hand, top of library, or straight to the battlefield.

pilot_tips.text: Fire Vampiric Tutor at the end step before your turn — the wish spends zero turns in transit and nobody gets a draw step to answer it.

captions.Green Sun's Zenith: **THE TEMPO WISH:** the only tutor here that pays tempo instead of charging it — Devoted Druid arrives on the battlefield, not in your hand.

departments.pull_quote: The fetch quests make you faster. They cannot make you broader.

departments.headline: THE TWO-MANA GUARANTEE
departments.dek: What is a command zone actually worth? Here: a turn-2 commander in 9,970 of 10,000 runs — a guarantee so cheap it rewrites your mulligan law. The Counselor reads the fine print; the Coach says when to pay the tax.
departments.body:
Begin with the exhibit everyone skips: the zone itself. Rule 903.8 lets you cast Hapatra from the command zone any time you could cast a sorcery — no draw required, no tutor spent. At two mana, that right gets exercised on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 seeded runs. The holding follows: your opening seven never needs her, so all seven cards are free to hunt the thing the zone cannot promise — a repeatable counter source.

The tax ladder above is the schedule: two more generic mana on each return trip (903.8). Read it against this deck's ledger — mean available mana 4.71 on turn 4, 6.15 on turn 6 — and a second or even third cast stays on schedule. So the court's spending advice: for Hapatra, pay the tax. Save Heroic Intervention and the boots for Yawgmoth and Mikaeus, the pieces the zone does not resurrect.

Colour identity (903.4) is the clause with teeth, and it counts mana symbols in rules text. Black-green admits every -1/-1 counter card on record and forbids the counterspell outright. Note what it does not forbid: green owns artifact and enchantment removal, and this 99 carries none. That hole is a signed trade, not a legal constraint — say so plainly in your Rule 0 conversation.

On the 21-point commander clock (903.10a), the record is short. Hapatra is an unevasive 2/2; eleven successful combats against a single defender is not a plan. Stack 001, step 11, classifies her combat trigger as a bonus iteration, never an engine. The clock exists. It is not yours.

Coach's corner (★): the political read. A two-mana commander behind a spread of 1/1 Snakes is the quietest opening in the format — the table files you under 'later.' That filing is an asset. Spend it on engine pieces, and expect it revoked the moment a tutor resolves.

captions.Hapatra, Vizier of Poisons: **THE GUARANTEE:** two mana, both colours, every single game — the one card your mulligan never has to find.

pilot_tips.text: Pay part of a taxed recast through Opal Palace — Hapatra returns wearing a +1/+1 counter per prior cast, big enough to outlive her own sweepers.

departments.pull_quote: The zone promises her. The seven cards in your hand are free to promise everything else.

departments.headline: RANK AND VILE
departments.dek: Sixty-four spells sort into one scarce class and a lot of abundance. The sources lead this roster because they have to — everything behind them is bodies becoming cards, and cards becoming a clock on every seat.

roster.role: The source — the class that is two deep
The converters — a clock on every seat

cards: Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER // Sephiroth, One-Winged Angel

roster.role: The combo shelf — two lines verified, the rest pending
Protection, recursion and the odd jobs

captions.Skullclamp: **THE ECONOMY:** every token here is a 1/1, so this is 'pay {1}, draw two' on repeat — the card that makes losing your board profitable.
captions.Obelisk Spider: **THE FAST CONVERTER:** it drains on counter placement, not death — roughly four times faster than any death-trigger drain on a loop.

pilot_tips.text: Mind the shroud: Greaves protects the Druid and locks Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting it — know which you want before you equip.

departments.headline: SCOUTED, NOT SIGNED
departments.dek: No sideboard means no incumbents: all ten are pool scouts, pulled from 11,831 eligible cards and ranked by what they add to the verified engines. Ayara and Warren Soultrader lead. And note what refuses to move — bracket 4 before, bracket 4 after, on every entry.

pilot_tips.text: Price the Monolith honestly: it makes colourless in a deck of double pips — the pool's cleanest scout does its job for zero mana and taps for colour.

departments.pull_quote: Every tagged line arrives wearing the same stamp — needs a stack scenario — because six lines that looked this good on paper are already refuted.

departments.headline: THIRTY-SIX LANDS, NONE TAPPED
departments.dek: How lopsided can a pip load get before the mana breaks? Black carries 71.4% of the pips on an even 50% source share and pays nothing for it: 29 black sources and 29 green against a target of 22, on curve 96.2% of the time on lands alone — and not one of the 36 lands arrives tapped.

captions.City of Brass: **THE INVOICE:** the price of a base this clean is written on your life total — City of Brass, Mana Confluence and Tarnished Citadel all charge you to fix.

pilot_tips.text: Point a spare -1/-1 counter at the Spirit you hand out — the Orchard's tax comes back as a Snake.

departments.pull_quote: Twenty-two lands make both colours and fourteen basics make one. Neither half can be the wrong half.

departments.headline: THE 2.007 COMMANDER
departments.dek: Mean cast turn 2.007 — Hapatra is on the table before most decks have finished introducing themselves. The rest of the ledger is what happens next, and what a simulation is not.

callouts.title: THE HEADLINE
callouts.text: Turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 runs; 99.9% by turn 6. She is the most reliable card in the book — which is exactly why the plan never worries about her.

callouts.title: THE REAL IDENTITY
callouts.text: 'Commander plus any -1/-1 payoff' assembles in 67.2% of runs at mean turn 3.62. That pair is the deck — the grindy median that out-cards three opponents.

callouts.title: THE HONEST CEILING
callouts.text: Hapatra plus Blowfly Infestation: 16.3% assembled, 12.5% by turn 6 — and unverified. Mikaeus plus a free outlet: 9.5%. The ceiling is real, narrow, and never the thing you mulligan toward.

departments.pull_quote: The goldfish models resource development, not games — and it still can't stop casting her on turn 2.

departments.headline: THE LOOP THAT MAKES NO MANA
departments.dek: The court affirms one true two-card infinite: Mikaeus and Devoted Druid, forever — four counter placements, one death, zero mana per cycle. It affirms a three-card Ballista kill beside it. And it strikes six pretenders from the record.

callouts.title: FIRST PASS PAYS
callouts.text: The turn they meet, the Druid's untap nets three green. Every later pass nets none: the returned Druid is a new object, and rule 302.6 silences its tap ability. The loop runs anyway — the untap cost carries no tap symbol, so 302.6 never touches it.

callouts.title: THE STEADY STATE
callouts.text: Four -1/-1 placements and one death per cycle, at zero mana. With Hapatra out, four Snakes. With Obelisk Spider, four table-wide drains. With Blood Artist, one life per cycle from a player of your choosing.

callouts.title: THE THIRD CARD
callouts.text: Mikaeus plus Walking Ballista is real, and it is three cards: the anthem holds a counterless Ballista at 1/1, so an external free outlet is mandatory. With one, unbounded damage — no drain payoff required.

callouts.title: THE STRIKEOUTS
callouts.text: Six listed pairings die on the record: the altars, the Feeder, the Seer, Yahenni and the Station each buy exactly one undying return, not a loop. And a sacrificed Snake buys zero — a token ceases to exist before its undying trigger is ever put on the stack.

captions.Devoted Druid: **EXHIBIT A:** its untap pays a -1/-1 counter as a cost — no tap symbol, so rule 302.6 never touches it. That technicality is the entire infinite.
captions.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: **THE HINGE:** undying powers both verified lines — and the same anthem may switch your own token loops off. That question tops the open docket.
captions.Walking Ballista: **THE CLOSER:** unbounded with Mikaeus and any free outlet — and never a two-card kill, because the anthem won't let it die on its own.

pilot_tips.text: Equip Greaves to net four green per cycle — and accept that shroud locks Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting the wearer.

departments.pull_quote: The database said nineteen. The record says: one true infinite, one three-card kill, six strikeouts, eleven open questions.
departments.note: Dossier pointer: FULL DOSSIER — JUDGE'S DESK, CASE A-001.

departments.headline: CASE A-001, READ TWICE
departments.dek: One seductive claim — that Hapatra's counter resets undying under Mikaeus — four resolver passes, four adversarial checks, verdict: pass. Every citation below is verbatim. The claim is false as written, and the findings are worth more than the claim.
departments.pull_quote: Where the record is silent, the record is silent — eleven lines remain open, and none may be spoken of as fact.

departments.headline: EIGHTY HANDS
departments.dek: Nobody painted this deck — eighty artists share its 88 cards, and no one holds more than three. So the credit goes to the whole field, led by the man who happened to paint both the signature sweeper and the verified kill piece.

featured.note:
Daniel Ljunggren tops this roster with three cards, and in an eighty-artist field that is not a signature — it is the crest of a perfectly flat wave. John Avon also has three. Nobody else clears two. The analysis says it plainly: no standout, so the honest feature is the breadth itself.

And the breadth has a cause worth stating out loud: nobody chose these printings. The decklist names cards, not editions, and each entry carries whatever printing the resolver returned first — which is why the largest single stamp is a reprint set holding twelve cards by twelve different artists, and why there is not one foil in the hundred. No curation happened here, and we won't invent taste where none was exercised.

What luck delivered is still worth the page. Ljunggren's three are Black Sun's Zenith, Forbidden Orchard and Walking Ballista — the deck's signature sweeper, its most mischievous land, and the verified kill piece. If one set of hands had to lead a flat field, the ledger could have done far worse.

also_worth_noting.note: Opal Palace and Spire of Industry are classic Avon architecture; Serrated Arrows is the odd one out — even the utility gets a landscape painter here.
Two cards, maximum gravity: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed — the combo hinge of the whole issue — and Eternal Witness, the rebuy that keeps the engine honest.
Chrome Mox and Worldly Tutor — two of the eleven Game Changers, one brush.

rhythm_notes: Five acts ride the depth ramp. Coach owns the high-energy cockpit and table acts (narrative, practice, participation, then three medium instruction/reference spreads). Act III cools into browsing (The 99) and imagination (The Short List) before the audits. The two dense Ledger sections — Sources Say and By the Numbers — sit either side of the declared full-bleed art break, and The Kill lands as the late narrative peak carrying the technical payload. Judge's Desk is buffered by narrative before and appreciation after; The Back Page closes low. No undeclared dense adjacency anywhere in the sequence.
gaps: decisions/ is empty, so What's Your Play? renders its standing TODO. Two spreads worth authoring: present-or-hold Yawgmoth into open mana, and Black Sun's Zenith rebuild versus Toxic Deluge panic with Blood Artist on board.

Eleven combo lines remain unresolved. Highest value: does Mikaeus's anthem switch the token loops off — the deck's two flagship engines may be mutually exclusive on the battlefield. Then the Blowfly family, Yawgmoth plus Hapatra as the realistic kill, Hapatra plus Host of the Hereafter, Necroskitter plus Black Sun's Zenith, and whether Heroic Intervention answers -X/-X effects.
Strategy DB topics flagged by the frame: auditing a combo list, the aristocrats outlet/fodder/converter taxonomy, counters-matter fundamentals, in-game tutor sequencing, and fast-mana trades.
No sideboard exists, so The Short List is all pool scouts. If Warren Soultrader and Gray Merchant of Asphodel ever land, Gravecrawler deserves a re-rank — the Zombie count would reach three.
